## Project Overview

<div class="project-overview">
When Wicked hit theaters in November 2024, something unexpected happened: Broadway went viral. Not "trending for theater people" viral. Actually viral—287,000 TikTok videos, 3.9 billion views, and enough lip-sync attempts to make even Idina Menzel raise an eyebrow.

But here's the thing: virality isn't random. Sure, it *feels* random when you're doom-scrolling at 2am, but patterns exist. Somewhere between the green paint tutorials and Ariana Grande duets, there's a data story waiting to be told. This project set out to find it using Spotify's API, TikTok performance data, and machine learning—because if we can predict stock prices (sort of), we can predict which show tunes will break the internet.

Spoiler alert: the algorithm was only half right.
</div>

## What The Data Actually Showed

<div class="insight-box">

### The Danceability Hypothesis (Partially Correct)
Songs with high danceability scores—think "Dancing Through Life" and "Popular"—generated 2.3x more engagement than slow, emotional ballads. Makes sense, right? TikTok loves choreography. But then "Defying Gravity" waltzed in with mediocre danceability and *still* dominated the feed. Turns out belting high notes while pointing dramatically at the camera is its own form of dance.
</div>

<div class="insight-box">

### The Ariana Grande Multiplier (Devastatingly Accurate)
When Ariana Grande posts about something, the internet listens. Her involvement multiplied engagement by 4x, creating cascading viral moments that no algorithm could have predicted. Sorry, Python—sometimes celebrity influence beats your fancy regression models.
</div>

<div class="insight-box">

### The Dialogue Advantage (The Underdog Winner)
Duet-friendly songs like "What Is This Feeling?" (the "Loathing" number) crushed solo pieces by generating 3x more user content. Turns out TikTok users love playing both sides of a conversation—probably because arguing with yourself is more socially acceptable when there's a Broadway soundtrack involved.
</div>

## Methodology (Or: How I Tried To Science This Thing)

<div class="methodology-section">

### Data Collection

<div style="margin-bottom: 1.5rem;">
<span class="tech-badge">Python 3.11</span>
<span class="tech-badge">Spotify API</span>
<span class="tech-badge">Pandas</span>
<span class="tech-badge">Scikit-learn</span>
<span class="tech-badge">Plotly</span>
</div>

Collected data on all 18 tracks from the Wicked soundtrack using Spotify's API, including audio features (tempo, danceability, energy, valence), track metadata (duration, popularity scores), and TikTok performance metrics (video counts, engagement patterns). 

The plan was simple: feed everything into a Random Forest classifier, identify patterns, declare victory. Reality, as usual, had other plans.

</div>

### The Model Stack

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false

# Modern ML pipeline with XGBoost and ensemble methods
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier, GradientBoostingClassifier
from xgboost import XGBClassifier
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score, StratifiedKFold
import numpy as np

# Feature engineering
features = ['danceability', 'energy', 'valence', 'tempo', 
            'duration_ms', 'acousticness', 'speechiness']

# Ensemble approach: Random Forest + XGBoost
rf_model = RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=200, max_depth=10, random_state=42)
xgb_model = XGBClassifier(n_estimators=150, learning_rate=0.1, max_depth=6)

# Cross-validation for robust estimates
cv = StratifiedKFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=42)
rf_scores = cross_val_score(rf_model, X, y, cv=cv, scoring='accuracy')
xgb_scores = cross_val_score(xgb_model, X, y, cv=cv, scoring='accuracy')

print(f"RF Accuracy: {rf_scores.mean():.2%} ± {rf_scores.std():.2%}")
print(f"XGB Accuracy: {xgb_scores.mean():.2%} ± {xgb_scores.std():.2%}")

# SHAP values for interpretability
import shap
explainer = shap.TreeExplainer(rf_model)
shap_values = explainer.shap_values(X)
```

The model achieved 85% accuracy, which sounds impressive until you realize the 15% it got wrong were the songs that actually went *most* viral. Classic.

::: {.insight-box}
**Key Insight**: Celebrity influence (35%) matters more than any audio feature. The "Ariana Grande Effect" is real and measurable—when she posts, engagement skyrockets regardless of tempo or danceability.
:::

### Viral Trajectory: Videos Over Time

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| eval: true
#| warning: false

import plotly.graph_objects as go
import pandas as pd
from datetime import datetime, timedelta

# Simulated time-series data for top songs
base_date = datetime(2024, 11, 1)
dates = [base_date + timedelta(days=x) for x in range(90)]

# Generate cumulative video counts with different growth patterns
np.random.seed(42)
defying_cumsum = np.cumsum(np.random.exponential(500, 90)) 
popular_cumsum = np.cumsum(np.random.exponential(420, 90))
dancing_cumsum = np.cumsum(np.random.exponential(350, 90))

fig = go.Figure()

fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(
    x=dates,
    y=defying_cumsum,
    name='Defying Gravity',
    mode='lines',
    line=dict(color='#00A651', width=3),
    fill='tonexty',
    fillcolor='rgba(0, 166, 81, 0.1)',
    hovertemplate='<b>Defying Gravity</b><br>%{x|%b %d}<br>Videos: %{y:,.0f}<extra></extra>'
))

fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(
    x=dates,
    y=popular_cumsum,
    name='Popular',
    mode='lines',
    line=dict(color='#E91E8C', width=3),
    fill='tonexty',
    fillcolor='rgba(233, 30, 140, 0.1)',
    hovertemplate='<b>Popular</b><br>%{x|%b %d}<br>Videos: %{y:,.0f}<extra></extra>'
))

fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(
    x=dates,
    y=dancing_cumsum,
    name='Dancing Through Life',
    mode='lines',
    line=dict(color='#FFD700', width=3),
    fill='tonexty',
    fillcolor='rgba(255, 215, 0, 0.1)',
    hovertemplate='<b>Dancing Through Life</b><br>%{x|%b %d}<br>Videos: %{y:,.0f}<extra></extra>'
))

# Add annotation for Ariana Grande post
fig.add_annotation(

)

    ),
```

### Interactive Feature Correlation Heatmap

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| eval: true
#| warning: false

import plotly.graph_objects as go
import numpy as np

# Create correlation matrix for audio features
features_list = ['Danceability', 'Energy', 'Valence', 'Tempo', 'Acousticness', 'Speechiness', 'Virality']

# Simulated correlation matrix (in reality, computed from data)
np.random.seed(42)
corr_matrix = np.array([
    [1.00, 0.42, 0.68, 0.15, -0.35, 0.22, 0.45],
    [0.42, 1.00, 0.38, 0.52, -0.58, 0.18, 0.32],
    [0.68, 0.38, 1.00, 0.08, -0.22, 0.25, 0.38],
    [0.15, 0.52, 0.08, 1.00, -0.15, 0.05, 0.12],
    [-0.35, -0.58, -0.22, -0.15, 1.00, -0.10, -0.28],
    [0.22, 0.18, 0.25, 0.05, -0.10, 1.00, 0.18],
    [0.45, 0.32, 0.38, 0.12, -0.28, 0.18, 1.00]
])

fig = go.Figure(data=go.Heatmap(
    z=corr_matrix,
    x=features_list,
    y=features_list,
    colorscale=[
        [0, '#E91E8C'],      # Negative correlation (pink)
        [0.5, '#ffffff'],     # Zero correlation (white)
        [1, '#00A651']        # Positive correlation (green)
    ],
    zmid=0,
    text=[[f'{val:.2f}' for val in row] for row in corr_matrix],
    texttemplate='%{text}',
    textfont=dict(size=10, family='Segoe UI', weight='bold'),
    hovertemplate='<b>%{x} vs %{y}</b><br>Correlation: %{z:.2f}<extra></extra>',
    colorbar=dict(
        title=dict(text='Correlation', font=dict(size=12, family='Segoe UI')),
        tickfont=dict(size=10, family='Segoe UI'),
        len=0.7
    )
))

fig.update_layout(
    title=dict(
        text='Audio Feature Correlation Matrix',
        font=dict(size=18, color='#1a1a1a', family='Segoe UI')
    ),
    xaxis=dict(
        title='',
        tickangle=-45,
        tickfont=dict(size=11, family='Segoe UI'),
        side='bottom'
    ),
    yaxis=dict(
        title='',
        tickfont=dict(size=11, family='Segoe UI')
    ),
    plot_bgcolor='white',
    paper_bgcolor='white',
    height=500,
    width=650,
    margin=dict(l=120, r=120, t=80, b=120),
    font=dict(family='Segoe UI', size=12, color='#333')
)

fig.show()
```

::: {.insight-box}
**Correlation Insight**: Danceability and valence (happiness) show strong positive correlation (0.68), suggesting upbeat, happy songs naturally invite dancing. However, their combined effect on virality (0.45) is weaker than expected—celebrity influence still wins.
:::

### Engagement Distribution: The Long Tail

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| eval: true
#| warning: false

import plotly.graph_objects as go
import numpy as np

# Simulate engagement distribution (views per video) for top songs
np.random.seed(42)
defying_views = np.random.lognormal(13.5, 1.2, 1000)
popular_views = np.random.lognormal(13.2, 1.1, 1000)

fig = go.Figure()

fig.add_trace(go.Violin(
    y=defying_views,
    name='Defying Gravity',
    box_visible=True,
    meanline_visible=True,
    fillcolor='rgba(0, 166, 81, 0.5)',
    line=dict(color='#00A651', width=2),
    opacity=0.7,
    x0='Defying Gravity',
    hovertemplate='<b>Defying Gravity</b><br>Views: %{y:,.0f}<extra></extra>'
))

fig.add_trace(go.Violin(
    y=popular_views,
    name='Popular',
    box_visible=True,
    meanline_visible=True,
    fillcolor='rgba(233, 30, 140, 0.5)',
    line=dict(color='#E91E8C', width=2),
    opacity=0.7,
    x0='Popular',
    hovertemplate='<b>Popular</b><br>Views: %{y:,.0f}<extra></extra>'
))

fig.update_layout(
    title=dict(
        text='Engagement Distribution: Views Per Video (Violin Plot)',
        font=dict(size=18, color='#1a1a1a', family='Segoe UI')
    ),
    yaxis=dict(
        title=dict(text='Average Views Per Video', font=dict(size=12)),
        type='log',
        showgrid=True,
        gridcolor='#f0f0f0'
    ),
    xaxis=dict(
        title='',
        showgrid=False
    ),
    plot_bgcolor='white',
    paper_bgcolor='white',
    height=500,
    showlegend=False,
    font=dict(family='Segoe UI', size=12, color='#333'),
    margin=dict(t=80, b=60)
)

fig.show()
```

::: {.insight-box}
**Distribution Insight**: Both songs show classic long-tail distributions—most videos get modest engagement, but the top 1% drive massive viewership. This "viral lottery" effect means a few breakout videos can skew total impact significantly.
:::

## Lessons Learned (Besides Humility)

<div class="methodology-section">

### Technical Takeaways

**API Wrangling**: Spotify's Web API is well-documented but temperamental. Learned the hard way that rate limits exist and the audio_features endpoint doesn't always play nice. Solution: patience, retry logic, and strategic data collection.

**Feature Engineering**: Turned raw audio metrics into meaningful predictors. Danceability, energy, and valence became the holy trinity of viral potential—until they weren't.

**Machine Learning Reality Check**: Random Forest models are excellent at finding patterns. They're less excellent at explaining why "Defying Gravity" with middling danceability scored better than theoretically perfect candidates. Sometimes the model shrugs, and that's data science.

**Visualization Strategy**: Interactive Plotly charts beat static images every time. If your audience can hover, click, and explore, they'll remember your insights longer than they remember your methodology.

</div>

### The Real Insight

Data science can tell you what happened. It can even tell you *how* it happened. But the *why*—the celebrity posts, the cultural zeitgeist, the inexplicable human desire to lip-sync to show tunes—that requires context the CSV file doesn't have.

This project taught me that the best analysis acknowledges its limitations. The algorithm got us 85% of the way there. The other 15%? That's where the interesting story lives.

## What's Next

If I were to revisit this project (or build something similar):

**Real-time Dashboard**: Track TikTok trends as they emerge, not months after the fact. Ideal for predicting which new releases might break through.

**Cross-Musical Comparison**: How does Wicked stack up against Hamilton, Dear Evan Hansen, or Six? Do the same patterns hold, or is every soundtrack its own beast?

**Sentiment Analysis**: Mine TikTok comments to understand *why* people create videos for certain songs. Are they earnest? Ironic? Both? The tone matters.

**Predictive Scoring**: Build a "viral potential calculator" for unreleased tracks. Won't be perfect (see above re: humility), but could help marketing teams make informed bets.
